title: Shoot First, Ask Questions Later? Building Rational Agents that Explore and Act Like People
claim: Strategic information seeking requires balancing questions against actions, with each role's reasoning modeled as inference over a hypothesis space.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right: Captain reasoning, central game scene, Spotter answer pipeline
description: A wide three-part hand-drawn-style illustration of the Collaborative Battleship game. The center shows a cartoon Captain (left) and Spotter (right) over a tilted isometric grid with colored ships. The Captain's thought bubble asks 'Is the purple ship vertical?' and the Spotter's answers 'No'. A small bubble reads 'G3'. Labels mark 'Visible to all' and 'Only visible to Spotter'. The left panel is the Captain's reasoning loop: an observation board feeds a generative world model that samples a hypothesis space of boards. A pink Decision diamond branches to Action (MAP argmax over a belief heatmap) or Question (argmax expected information gain, with a density plot). The right panel shows the Spotter's full board, the question, and the answer, with a code snippet that translates language to code. Blue and pastel colors dominate.
caption: Illustration of our Collaborative Battleship game. On each turn, the Captain must choose whether to gather information (ask a question) or take action (shoot at a tile). The Spotter sees the full board, but can only provide yes/no answers. Each role requires well-defined forms of internal reasoning (thought bubbles), which we implement as Monte Carlo inference over an approximate hypothesis space. This framework allows us to compare both humans and LM agents against idealized Bayesian strategies in a controlled setting.
abstract: Many emerging applications of AI--from scientific discovery to medical diagnosis--require agents to seek information strategically: forming hypotheses, asking targeted questions, and making decisions under uncertainty. In high-stakes settings with limited resources, do language models (LMs) behave like rational agents? Drawing on insights from human cognition, we develop methods to evaluate and enhance agentic information-seeking. First, we introduce a decision-oriented dialogue task called Collaborative Battleship, in which a Captain must balance exploration (asking questions) and action (taking shots), while a Spotter must supply accurate, contextually-grounded answers. Compared to human players (N=42), we find that many LM agents struggle to ask informative questions, produce accurate answers, and identify high-utility actions. To address these gaps, we develop novel Monte Carlo inference strategies for LMs inspired by Bayesian Experimental Design (BED). For Spotter agents, our approach boosts accuracy by up to 14.7% absolute over LM-only baselines; for Captain agents, it raises expected information gain (EIG) by up to 0.227 bits (94.2% of the achievable noise ceiling). Combined, these components yield sharper targeting (+0.303-0.374 F1), and enable weaker LMs, such as Llama-4-Scout, to outperform both humans (8% -> 82% win rate) and frontier models (0% -> 67% win rate vs. GPT-5) at ~1% of GPT-5's cost. We replicate these findings on Guess Who?, where our methods significantly boost accuracy (+28.3-42.4 p.p.), demonstrating their general applicability for building information-seeking agents.
